data.title: Amid Nvidia saga, T-Head IPO crucial for Alibaba – and Chinese AIAnalysts say the spin-off is more than just a litmus test for Alibaba’s valuation and a potential boost to its AI growth plans.
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding’s planned Hong Kong listing of its semiconductor design arm, T-Head, is poised to reshape China’s artificial intelligence hardware arena while unlocking billions of dollars in trapped valuation for the tech titan, according to analysts.
The proposed spin-off serves as a test of whether the sum of Alibaba’s parts is worth significantly more than its current market valuation. Alibaba’s Hong Kong-listed shares slipped about 1 per cent to HK$100.60 on Wednesday, the day following the announcement.
“The chip business was previously hidden within Alibaba Cloud and difficult to price independently,” said analysts at Chinese financial data provider Wind, in a research note on Wednesday. “Once listed separately, it becomes a new yardstick for whether Alibaba is undervalued.”
T-Head is one of the first Alibaba stand-alone units to pursue an initial public offering (IPO) in the last few years, and represents a major public-market pricing test for a Chinese AI hardware infrastructure provider.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
T-Head is seeking to raise between US$2 billion and US$3 billion, Reuters reported earlier this week. If achieved, that sum could surpass the combined proceeds raised by domestic makers of graphics processing units Biren Technology and Iluvatar CoreX, which listed in Hong Kong earlier this year, according to Wind analysts.
The injection of independent funding would relieve pressure on Alibaba’s balance sheet, analysts said.
Founded in 2018, T-Head remains closely tied to Alibaba Cloud and has relied heavily on profits from the group’s core e-commerce business. Last month, Alibaba chairman and co-founder Joe Tsai said that the company was using US$25 billion in free cash flow generated by its online shopping operations to fund AI infrastructure and model development.
“We believe the spin-off can unlock the value of T-Head and allow it to access capital independently,” said Jefferies analysts Thomas Chong and Zoey Zong on Wednesday, adding that the transaction would help investors “better assess and value the retained group” while pricing T-Head “on its own merits”.
Listings by Chinese chip companies underscore an accelerating drive towards domestic semiconductor self-sufficiency backed by private capital. The trend comes amid intensified anxiety over China’s future access to advanced silicon amid heightened scrutiny following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair and an expected post-midterm push in the US Congress for stricter trade policies.
In-house chip design could provide Alibaba with a degree of strategic insulation against growing headwinds.
T-Head “mitigates this risk and differentiates Alibaba from Chinese hyperscalers more reliant on external supply”, Morgan Stanley analysts said in a research note on Wednesday.
A key pillar expected to underpin T-Head’s valuation is the commercialisation progress of its flagship AI processors, particularly the Zhenwu M890 and the latest V900.
Unveiled in September and billed as “the most powerful AI chip in China today”, the V900 was said to deliver three times the performance of its predecessor.
Alibaba claimed a computing cluster powered by the V900 could link up to 500,000 chips to handle both training and inference for frontier AI models. Mass production and commercial availability were scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

data.title: Hong Kong arts group urges balance in funding criteria as attendance falls
data.description:
A major Hong Kong performing arts group has urged the government to give greater weight to qualitative measures when setting funding criteria for local organisations, arguing that changing social trends have contributed to falling attendance.
Celina Chin Man-wah, executive director of the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra, also warned on Thursday that the group might have to scale back its community work to devote more resources to income-generating or sponsored activities.
Her comments followed the announcement on Wednesday of further details of a government overhaul of funding for major performing arts groups, linking subsidies more closely to performance and artistic merit.
“It’s appropriate to measure performance in both quantitative and qualitative standards, but we have to pay attention to the split of how much each takes. It’s a topic that requires discussion and looking into,” Chin said on a radio programme.
“We’ve always said it’s very important to use the right metrics to measure [the achievements of] an arts group. If we used the wrong yardstick, it’d be very dangerous.”
Under the new funding mechanism, each group’s annual allocation will comprise a “baseline subvention” and a “performance-based subvention”. The baseline component will gradually fall from about 77 per cent of the total to 50 per cent.

The performance-based component will take into account each group’s non-government revenue, including box-office takings, other operating income, donations and sponsorship, as well as its achievement of key performance indicators.
The mechanism applies only to designated “major performing arts groups”.
Nine currently hold that status, the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra, Hong Kong Sinfonietta, Hong Kong Ballet, Hong Kong Dance Company, City Contemporary Dance Company, Hong Kong Repertory Theatre, Chung Ying Theatre Company and Zuni Icosahedron.
Under the reforms, groups with exceptional performance may receive more funding, while those that underperform will face cuts. Groups that consistently fail to meet the required standards will lose their “major” status.
Authorities said the groups would have a five-year transition period, with the reforms fully implemented from 2032–33.
The government said the changes aimed to encourage major groups to innovate continuously, while allowing capable medium-sized groups with consistently outstanding performance to gain major status and the associated funding.
Over the past two decades, annual government funding for the nine major groups has risen from about HK$220 million to about HK$450 million (US$57.3 million), an increase of more than 104 per cent.
Over the same period, however, the government said total paid attendance at the groups’ performances had fallen from 360,000 to 310,000, while the overall attendance rate had dropped from about 77 per cent to 69 per cent.

Chin attributed part of the decline to broader changes in Hong Kong beyond the arts and cultural sector, including falling birth rates, residents’ growing preference for spending across the border and a post-pandemic shift towards staying out less late.
With less baseline funding, she said, the orchestra might have to devote more resources to attracting audiences. That could mean scaling back unsponsored community activities, such as visits and classes for people undergoing rehabilitation.
Chin stressed that artistic work often needed time to gain recognition. Some compositions that were ahead of their time might initially be poorly received by audiences and performers, she said, only to become staples of the repertoire years later.
“We’d be worried, as we have to balance our books and we might not be able to recoup our costs in a short time frame. I can’t say it would stifle creative development, but it’s a message that we’d have to pass on to the artists,” she said.
But lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung said the reforms would support the sector’s healthy development and provide a “funding ladder” for small and medium-sized groups seeking major status.
Asked how long a group’s performance should be deemed “consistently unsatisfactory” before it lost that status, Ip suggested about three years. He said there should be a gradual transition rather than an abrupt funding cut.

data.title: Li Ka-shing family’s British pub chain names first female CEO in 227 years
data.description:
Greene King, the British brewer and pub operator owned by Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-shing’s family, has appointed its first female chief executive in its 227-year history, seven years after the family acquired the business as part of its overseas expansion.
Clair Preston-Beer, currently Greene King’s chief commercial officer, will take over the role in March 2027, succeeding Nick Mackenzie, who will step down at the end of February but remain on the company’s board to support the transition, CK Asset, the investment group founded by Li Ka-shing said on Thursday.
Greene King has operated in Britain’s traditionally male-dominated pub and brewing industry since 1799.
Preston-Beer joined Greene King in 2020 and has held several senior positions, including managing director of its pub business and chief operating officer. She has more than 27 years of experience in retail and leisure, including nearly 17 years at Costa Coffee, Britain’s largest coffee chain.
Founded in Bury St Edmunds, Greene King now operates about 2,500 pubs, restaurants and hotels across England, Wales and Scotland, employs around 38,000 people and owns about 90 per cent of its operating properties.
CK Asset acquired the company in 2019 for £2.7 billion (US$3.58 billion), in a deal that valued the business at £4.6 billion, including debt. The purchase came amid uncertainty over Britain’s departure from the European Union and a weakened pound, as the Li family bet on the resilience of the country’s pub culture and added an extensive property portfolio to their overseas investments.
The acquisition was consistent with the family’s reputation for timing investments and disposals around market cycles, often buying established businesses when sentiment is weak and selling assets when valuations are favourable.
The brewer also has a connection to China. Its Greene King IPA gained popularity there after Chinese President Xi Jinping was photographed drinking a pint with then British Prime Minister David Cameron during a 2015 state visit.
The acquisition reflected CK Asset’s preference for businesses with established assets and recurring cash flows. The group also has interests in British water and energy utilities, Australian electricity and gas networks, renewable energy and Canadian property services.
Overseas operations contributed about 63 per cent of CK Asset’s profit in the first half of 2026, compared with nearly 37 per cent from Hong Kong and mainland China, according to its 2026 interim results.
CK Asset executive committee member Gerald Ma said Preston-Beer’s appointment reflected the company’s succession planning and her familiarity with Greene King’s operations.

data.title: Hong Kong passes bill to speed up development of Northern Metropolis megaproject
data.description:
Hong Kong’s legislature has given the green light to legislation aimed at expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis megaproject near the border with mainland China, with the government saying the bill will help achieve targets in the city’s first five-year plan.
Lawmakers completed the third reading of the Northern Metropolis Development Bill and unanimously passed it on Thursday. The bill resumed a second reading on Wednesday, with lawmakers debating it for about eight hours over the two days.
Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Thursday that the Northern Metropolis Development Bill would lay a solid foundation for achieving the vision of the megaproject as laid out in the plan, which outlines Hong Kong’s socio-economic development between 2026 and 2030 to align with the national blueprint.
“We have explicitly stated in the first five-year plan a binding target of producing 900 hectares of spade-ready land in the Northern Metropolis to facilitate the development of industry, housing and public facilities,” Linn said at the Legislative Council meeting.
“At this critical moment of going all out, the passage of the bill will give us strong confidence to achieve this binding target.”
She also said the passage of the bill would help open a promising chapter for the development of the Northern Metropolis under the plan, which envisioned the megaproject as a high-quality hub for education, innovation and technology, industry development and talent.
Linn said the Legco managed to pass the bill one-and-a-half months earlier than the government’s initial schedule, demonstrating its contribution to expediting the megaproject and a positive interaction between the executive and legislative branches.
The bill, which applies only to the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis, focuses on streamlining town planning procedures, expediting land resumption compensation payments, accelerating construction work and easing cross-border flows of people, goods, data and capital.
It also states provisions for statutory corporations and empowers the Executive Council, the government’s key decision-making body, to create subsidiary legislation for future measures.
The government plans to table subsidiary legislation in stages, with the first stage including measures to ease immigration procedures at the cross-border innovation and technology park in the Lok Ma Chau Loop.
Subsidiary legislation handling other cross-border flow elements will be dealt with in subsequent stages.

Election Committee lawmaker Maggie Chan Man-ki said she hoped the government would establish subsidiary legislation regulating cross-border data flow as soon as possible, given that innovation and technology (I&T) was the megaproject’s focus.
She added that Hong Kong had to define important data and introduce a mechanism to protect information classified into different tiers to align with standards and practices in mainland China.
Chan stressed that such an arrangement should be stipulated under the law, rather than stated in a guideline, to boost deterrence.
Fellow Election Committee legislator Andrew Lam Siu-lo acknowledged the government’s efforts to expedite the megaproject, but warned that departments and bureaus should work together to prevent development projects from being held up by individual approval procedures.
He urged the government to publish its operational guidelines, deal with project applications through a single platform, and set out approval timelines and key performance indicators.
Lawmaker Webster Ng Kam-wah, representing the accountancy sector, suggested that the government provide details on the arrangements for disclosing the financial status of statutory corporations, as well as on the administration’s potential commitments for such companies.

He noted that tax incentives to attract leading enterprises to set up operations there would be dealt with in a separate ordinance and urged the government to table proposals as soon as possible.
The relevant bills committee earlier scrutinised the legislation for about 30 hours between July and October.
Beijing has tasked Hong Kong with expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis – envisioned as a new economic engine and housing hub – in the nation’s 15th five-year plan, which runs from 2026 to 2030.

data.title: ‘Web of complexity’: Jensen Huang’s position in doubt as Nvidia shares plunge
data.description:
Nvidia shares fell more than 8 per cent at one point in US after-hours trading on Wednesday as CEO Jensen Huang’s prospects of hanging onto his role became more clouded after media reports of a board meeting and another extramarital affair.
The drop in the American AI chip giant’s share price erased a 2.9 per cent rebound in the regular trading session, after the stock lost over 9.5 per cent in trading on Monday and Tuesday.
It came as speculation mounted over whether Huang would keep his job. Nvidia’s board was preparing to remove him and could meet as soon as Wednesday to decide his future, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing informed sources.
Separately, The New York Times reported that Huang – who had already admitted to marital infidelity, with media reports linking him to Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang – also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, who reported to him. The newspaper cited five people who had worked at the company as sources.
Nvidia declined to comment.

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at US-based merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co, said in a note issued on Wednesday that Jensen Huang might not last long.
“In our view, the writing is on the wall that Jensen’s days at Nvidia could be numbered and we would expect this to be a very fluid situation over the next 48 hours,” he said.
“Jensen has created a black-eye moment for himself and Nvidia and now has created a spider web of complexity that Wall Street, Silicon Valley, [Washington], and the global tech ecosystem are trying to figure out what is next.
“While Jensen is the hearts and lungs of the Nvidia story, the company and its leading edge GPU technology will go on and it does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the ‘AI Revolution’ chip arms race.”
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk weighed in on X, saying that it would be “an honor” to hire Jensen Huang if the Nvidia board ousted the company’s founder.

@zerohedge That would be an honor
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 12, 2026

On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation after Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair, amid reports that he had allegedly been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
The public storm has threatened to undermine Jensen Huang’s standing as one of corporate America’s most visible champions for preserving US semiconductor trade ties with China.
It could also intensify Washington’s tech blockade on China following the Democratic Party’s victory in midterm elections this month, which analysts said could give the US Congress the political momentum needed to plug loopholes in existing semiconductor restrictions, accelerating efforts to curb third-country chip smuggling and cutting off Chinese tech firms from overseas cloud computing clusters.
Brian Colello, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said the fallout had not crept into Nvidia’s financial outlook, because near- and medium-term demand for its chips remained high amid the artificial intelligence boom.
“We think Nvidia’s wide moat is underpinned by high switching costs around its CUDA AI software ecosystem, and hardware and networking product design expertise,” Colello said. “These assets should enable Nvidia to keep building best-of-breed data centre products, regardless of the CEO.”

data.title: ICAC charges team leader of Kai Tak Hospital subcontractor over extortion
data.description:
Hong Kong’s anti-corruption watchdog has charged a subcontractor’s team leader for allegedly extorting more than HK$75,000 (US$9,600) from five electrical workers at the Kai Tak Hospital site, vowing to work with the government to strengthen protections for imported labour.
According to an Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) statement on Thursday, Zeng Chusong, the 52-year-old site team leader from Billion Best (E&M) Engineering Company, faced 10 counts of an agent accepting an advantage for allegedly soliciting payment to secure and maintain employment for the workers.
“The ICAC maintains a zero-tolerance policy towards corruption and will continue to collaborate with the Development Bureau and other stakeholders to prevent the recurrence of crimes similar to this case,” the commission said.
It added that Zeng, a site team leader for a subcontractor of the Kai Tak Hospital construction project in central Kowloon, had his case scheduled for mention at Tuen Mun Court on Thursday morning after being charged on Wednesday night.
Zeng was charged with extorting HK$75,100 from five imported electrical workers between September and November 2026.
Due to a labour shortage in the construction industry, main contractor China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) Limited applied for an importation quota through the Labour Importation Scheme for Construction Sector for its subcontractors, including the defendant and the five electrical workers referred to work on the project, the ICAC added.
The investigation revealed that the daily salary of the five electrical workers was HK$1,300, and that they paid Zeng amounts ranging from HK$9,000 to HK$23,600 out of fear that they would lose their jobs.
To strengthen imported workers’ understanding of anti-corruption laws in Hong Kong, corruption prevention talks would be arranged for workers within eight weeks of their arrival, the commission said.

The watchdog urged construction workers who were approached for payment in exchange for employment to refuse immediately and report the crime to its 24-hour hotline at 2526 6366.
The ICAC said both the main contractor and Billion Best strictly prohibited their employees or agents from soliciting or accepting advantages from others in relation to their affairs and business.
The commission added that China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) and the subcontractor had cooperated fully with its investigation.

data.title: Next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment advances: does the evidence match the hype?Three hospitals are planning to test the treatment on 30 patients with kidney cancer.
data.description:
Hong Kong is expanding clinical trials of histotripsy, a non-invasive treatment that uses focused ultrasound to destroy tumours, as the city seeks to establish a role in developing the technology for kidney cancer.
The CUHK Medical Centre, Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong and Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital would begin trials involving 30 patients targeting kidney cancer, the Li Ka Shing Foundation said on Wednesday.
The trials mark the latest development in Hong Kong business tycoon Li Ka-shing’s biotech investments, which have drawn international attention. “Hong Kong [becomes] the first city in Asia to validate the safety and efficacy of treating renal diseases with histotripsy,” the tycoon’s charity said in an emailed statement.
Histotripsy uses high-intensity focused ultrasound waves to break down cancer cells into a harmless liquefied substance that the body can absorb within months. The US Food and Drug Administration cleared the technology for treating live tumours in 2023, while clinical trials are exploring its use against kidney cancer in the UK and the US.
More than 400 patients in Hong Kong had successfully received histotripsy treatment, according to the foundation. Gleneagles has successfully completed 20 procedures on pancreatic cancer since trials began in March, while the CUHK Medical Centre has completed six cases since June.
The Li Ka Shing Foundation has increased its support for the treatment in recent years, citing its “groundbreaking” potential as a “non-invasive, painless and highly effective” option for cancer patients.
Since 2024, the charity has donated three histotripsy systems, each valued at US$3 million, to the University of Hong Kong’s Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Faculty of Medicine and Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital.
In May, the foundation announced that it would subsidise treatment fees for 200 patients over the next three years. Eligible patients can undergo the procedure for HK$50,000 (US$6,372), compared with a typical cost of about HK$260,000.
Despite the growing excitement around histotripsy, clinical evidence supporting its wider use was still in its early stages, according to researchers including Hop S Tran Cao, associate professor of surgical oncology at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Centre.
In a paper published in September, the researchers described the technology as a “genuine advance” but cautioned that there was limited evidence to draw “definitive conclusions regarding its true clinical value”. They added that “public enthusiasm and commercial promotion” had moved faster than the available clinical evidence.
Broader use of focused ultrasound is also advancing internationally. Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, recently launched a first-in-human clinical trial investigating whether low-intensity focused ultrasound could be used to reduce auditory hallucinations in people with schizophrenia.
In June, the University of Virginia said researchers had used focused ultrasound to deliver therapeutic microRNAs in an experimental study to treat brain cancer in mice.

data.title: UK eases BN(O) visa barriers for Hong Kong protesters convicted over 2019 unrest
data.description:
The UK government has confirmed that convictions linked to Hong Kong’s 2019 protests should generally not prevent otherwise eligible applicants from using the British National (Overseas) visa scheme, following reports that several convicted protesters had their applications rejected.
In a letter on Wednesday to Alex Sobel, chairman of the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said there would now be a “presumption in favour” of ensuring that protest-related convictions did not prevent otherwise eligible applicants from using the scheme.
“The government recognises that many of those involved in the protests are among the individuals the route was intended to support,” she said.
Under the change, applicants who fail to meet the scheme’s standard suitability requirements because of their participation in the protests will automatically be considered by ministers for “leave outside the immigration rules”.
Mahmood said the Home Office was establishing a formal process, backed by published guidance, to ensure such cases could be “identified and considered consistently”.

She described the move as a “targeted measure” reflecting Hong Kong’s particular circumstances, saying it did not change the government’s broader approach to criminality within the immigration system.
“We will continue to reserve the right to refuse an application in circumstances where we believe criminal behaviour is serious enough that it should preclude admission to the United Kingdom,” she said.
Under current Home Office rules, a conviction resulting in a prison sentence of 12 months or more, including a suspended sentence, generally triggers mandatory refusal of entry or settlement.
The announcement followed a September report by British newspaper Metro, which cited lawyers as saying that at least 12 Hongkongers convicted over the 2019 protests had been refused visas under the scheme since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.
Britain introduced the visa scheme for Hongkongers following the enactment of the city’s national security law in 2020. More than 187,000 people have been issued BN(O) visas since the scheme opened in 2021.

data.title: Chinese firms can boost valuation using buy-backs, payouts: Goldman Sachs
data.description:
Chinese companies could unlock a further 15 per cent in equity valuation upside by stepping up share buy-backs and dividend payouts, as Beijing seeks to encourage listed firms to return more cash to investors, according to Goldman Sachs.
The US investment bank said in a report on Wednesday that an increase in corporate payout ratios and share repurchases, in line with policymakers’ efforts to improve shareholder returns, could lift valuations of the MSCI China Index by about 15 per cent from current levels through improved returns on equity and cash distributions to shareholders.
Goldman said Chinese companies had historically favoured issuing new shares over buying them back, with equity issuance outpacing repurchases for most of the past two decades.
The resulting net share issuance had diluted earnings per share by about 15 per cent cumulatively, weighing on shareholder returns, according to the report.
The imbalance has persisted alongside deteriorating corporate profitability. Return on equity among Chinese listed companies had declined for six consecutive years, while realised earnings per share growth had fallen short of market expectations for nine years in a row, the bank said.
Chinese equities had underperformed global markets by 110 percentage points since 2020, reflecting subdued earnings growth and a sharp contraction in valuations, according to the bank. The MSCI China Index’s price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 9.7 times from 17 times at its previous cycle peak in early 2021.
The report came as Chinese regulators earlier this month sought to encourage companies to buy back shares and support the stock market amid sluggish corporate profitability and weak investor confidence, including lowering the interest rate on a central bank relending programme by 25 basis points to 1 per cent and removing some restrictions on share buy-backs.
The measures were announced following a joint meeting of the People’s Bank of China, the China Securities Regulatory Commission and other financial regulators on November 2, as authorities sought to stabilise the stock market after a big sell-off in October.
On the mainland, the CSI 300 Index slumped 8.5 per cent last month, its biggest monthly decline in more than a decade, while the Shanghai Composite Index dropped 6.3 per cent.
Goldman expected Chinese companies to deliver annualised earnings-per-share growth of about 10 per cent and a normalised return on equity of 12 per cent over the next five years, supported by artificial intelligence, a trend of “going global” and policies aimed at curbing excessive competition.
The bank also saw scope for a valuation re-rating of about 10 per cent as corporate profitability normalises, even without the additional boost from higher shareholder payouts.

data.title: Charity helps neurodivergent people build confidence through nutrition, dance
data.description:
For 33-year-old Coco Choi Pak-yin and 24-year-old Crystal Lee Wing-wai, few things bring more joy than dancing at the Hong Kong charity Love 21 Foundation.
As neurodivergent individuals, they take part in a variety of tailored nutrition and sports programmes offered by the organisation, including dance classes. Through dance, they have found a space to connect with others and express themselves, and gained the confidence to showcase their talent in public.
“Compared with before, she is much more confident and outgoing now,” Crystal’s father, Lee Tak-wai, said.
Located in San Po Kong, Love 21 was founded by CEO Jeff Rotmeyer nine years ago and supports nearly 700 members with Down’s syndrome, autism or other neurodivergent conditions. The charity is a beneficiary of the annual fundraising campaign Operation Santa Claus (OSC), with its three-year partnership ending this year.
“Playing sports and getting nutritional advice are things that we all need as human beings … We believe that before we judge any human being by their ability, we first have to make sure that they have real opportunities to reach their potential,” Rotmeyer said.
The foundation offers a wide range of programmes, including nearly 1,000 classes a month and around 100 types of activities, to help members uncover their talent, develop confidence and pursue their passions.
Rotmeyer said funding from OSC had enabled Love 21 to identify serious diet-related challenges faced by some of the families it serves and offer them further nutritional and dietary support and care.
“I’ve been eating less meat and more fish and vegetables, as well as drinking more calcium-rich milk,” Crystal Lee said.

Chan Fung-hing, Choi’s mother, noticed that her daughter was now more willing to drink water and had healthier-looking skin.
While the organisation has made progress with its programmes, Rotmeyer said challenges remain to improve awareness and combat social stigma against neurodivergent people.
“This is a beautiful community who are living all around us here in Hong Kong, but they do not feel safe and accepted in our society,” he said.
Rotmeyer explained that people with neurodivergent conditions sometimes found it difficult to control their emotions or behaviour and, for many of them, stepping out into Hong Kong’s busy streets could be intimidating as they were often confronted with stares, whispers and judgment from strangers.
Carers also said taking neurodivergent people out in public could be stressful.
“It’s not that they intentionally behave that way. Sometimes they simply cannot control [their outbursts],” said Coco’s mother, Chan Fung-hing.
Rotmeyer said one of the charity’s goals was to create more opportunities for members to showcase their talent and contribute to society through public events. To this end, the organisation staged its first Celebration of Ability show in December 2025.

Crystal Lee was one of the emcees at last year’s show, which was held at Y Square in Chai Wan. Both she and Choi also took part in a dance item and are set to return to the stage this year in what Rotmeyer hopes will become an annual event.
“Watching Crystal is truly inspiring. I never imagined she could do so well and handle the pressure of hosting an event like this,” Chan said. “It’s really not easy. Even people [without disabilities] would find it challenging.”
Rotmeyer said many people in Hong Kong had never interacted with someone with a neurodivergent condition. Through the event, he hoped audiences would gain a better understanding of the abilities and potential of people with intellectual disabilities.
“We hope they will come and fill the theatre with enthusiasm and appreciation for our members’ talents,” he said.
Established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988, OSC has raised over HK$415 million and supported more than 382 charitable projects across Hong Kong, benefiting more than 100,000 people.

data.title: Register or else: Houthi rebels’ fresh demands put Chinese firms in a dilemma
data.description:
The escalating conflicts between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels in Yemen have put many listed Hong Kong and mainland Chinese companies in a dilemma, especially as the Houthis order foreign businesses to register with a local body to avoid becoming targets of military strikes.
The situation requires “serious attention” from businesses with a presence in the oil-rich region, according to an analyst focusing on the issue.
The Iran-backed rebel militia recently warned that foreign companies operating in Saudi Arabia should register with the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Centre (HOCC) – a body set up by the Houthis in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa – to protect their facilities from future attacks, according to China’s state-run Xinhua News Agency.
“The warning warrants serious attention, particularly near ports and energy facilities,” said Naser al-Tamimi, a senior associate research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies.
“Chinese ownership or a Hong Kong listing does not automatically confer exemption.”
A variety of Hong Kong-listed companies, many of them Chinese-owned, operate in Saudi Arabia and could be affected by the conflict.
CK Hutchison Holdings, the Hong Kong-listed conglomerate founded by tycoon Li Ka-shing, operates a port in the Saudi city of Jazan through a subsidiary.
H World Group – a Chinese hotel management company also listed in Hong Kong – operates in Saudi Arabia and plans to open a new hotel in the capital city Riyadh next year.
WeRide, the Hong Kong-listed Chinese autonomous driving company, launched a robotaxi pilot programme in Saudi Arabia last year and has plans to proceed with a wider commercial roll-out.
Beijing previously liaised with the Houthis to seek safe passage for Chinese ships in the Red Sea after the rebel militia declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, according to Reuters. The Chinese government does not formally recognise the Houthis.

But registration with the HOCC was “not automatically legal”, al-Tamimi said, adding that companies would need to conduct “careful legal and security assessments” before engaging.
“The obstacles include sanctions-related compliance risks, potential Saudi objections, disclosure of sensitive locations, and joint-venture obligations,” al-Tamimi said.
As regional tensions escalate, Hong Kong and Chinese businesses in Saudi Arabia could face rising insurance costs and disruptions to logistics and investments, according to al-Tamimi.
On Sunday, a tower in Riyadh’s business district was damaged in an aerial attack claimed by the Houthis. Two missile attacks on the capital were intercepted on Tuesday.
“The warning alone is unlikely to disrupt broader Chinese-Saudi cooperation,” al-Tamimi said. But continued Houthi strikes could “expose Beijing’s limited ability to shield Chinese assets from regional conflict”, he added.
Other high-profile companies with exposure to the region include J&T Global Express, a Hong Kong-listed logistics provider whose subsidiary provides shipping services in Saudi Arabia.
China National Petroleum Corporation – the state-owned parent of PetroChina – also has operations in Saudi Arabia through its subsidiary, China Petroleum Pipeline Engineering.

data.title: Losing steam? Hong Kong hit by run of lacklustre IPOs amid tepid investor demand
data.description:
Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market has endured a tough few days, with all six listings launched this week priced at or near the bottom of their marketed ranges amid tepid institutional interest.
Chinese memory product maker Hosin Electronics and Xiaomi-backed chipmaker Zhuhai Amicro Technology became the latest firms to debut on the city’s stock market on Thursday, joining Hong Kong’s busiest week for IPOs in months after a sluggish August-to-October stretch.
Both firms trimmed their valuations to get across the finish line. Amicro priced its shares at HK$9.9 (US$1.26), close to the bottom of its HK$9.27 to HK$11.58 indicative range. Hosin set its offer price at HK$72.83, also hugging the floor of its HK$72.29 to HK$82.90 range.
While both drew strong retail oversubscription, institutional appetite remained tepid, with Hosin and Amicro’s international offerings only oversubscribed by 0.45 and 0.05 times, respectively.
Yet pricing low to lure buyers and ensure smooth debuts offered little shield against early selling pressure. Hosin opened flat in early trading after raising HK$1.07 billion.
Amicro, in contrast, opened 37 per cent higher after raising HK$700 million.
A total of six companies had gone public in Hong Kong this week as of Thursday. The other four – graphics processing unit maker Suzhou Denglin Technology, chip packaging and testing company Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology, RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology and Sichuan Neautus Traditional Chinese Medicine – were all similarly priced at or near the bottom of their ranges.
Denglin, the week’s largest listing, saw its international offering oversubscribed by just 0.34 times after pricing itself at the bottom of its range. It fell 10 per cent in its first two trading days after raising HK$1.4 billion.
Chinese medicine maker Neautus’ retail tranche was oversubscribed nearly 2,190 times, but its international tranche was only 0.25 times oversubscribed. It rose 27.6 per cent on its debut on Wednesday, after being priced at the bottom of its range at HK$40.2.
“Investors are more cautious and selective these days,” said Kenny How Sze-ming, council member at the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association. “Demand is simply not that overwhelming, pushing deals towards the lower end.”

data.title: When AI agents go rogue, who can Hong Kong hold accountable?
data.description:
When OpenAI’s AI agents launched an autonomous attack on Australia’s Medicare portal in June, it took the company 84 days to report what had happened – a delay that exposed gaps in regulatory oversight that Hong Kong industry experts say the city must also address.
The incident followed breaches involving Google’s Gemini AI, which compromised three companies a month earlier. Google did not confirm those breaches until September, and only in response to media questions.
Such incidents have drawn scrutiny from authorities around the world, prompting efforts to regulate AI agents and clarify responsibility for their actions.
Singapore released the world’s first official guidelines on AI agents earlier this year, with security agencies in the UK, mainland China and the United States quickly following suit.
A Hong Kong industry association plans to release its own guidelines this week, ahead of a government framework expected in the middle of next year. Local experts said the city had to also address gaps in reporting requirements, human oversight and legal liability.
Legal accountability
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced plans for official guidelines on AI agent management in his policy address in September. The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau told the South China Morning Post it aimed to publish them in the middle of next year.
The Department of Justice said government bureaus and departments had largely completed a preliminary review of more than 600 ordinances. A further review would begin shortly to examine legal liability for accidents caused by AI products.
Legal experts and industry leaders have called for the proposed framework to clearly define accountability and require human oversight.
Adrian Mak Ho-ting, chief of staff for global affairs at AI Safety Asia, said Hong Kong’s legal framework had clear gaps in reporting requirements, with obligations falling on victims rather than the developers or deployers of the agents responsible.
Mak, a lawyer who teaches media and AI law at the University of Hong Kong, said the newly enacted Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance required affected operators to report serious security breaches to the government within 12 hours and other incidents within 48 hours.

“That duty only falls on the operator victim and not on the person who perpetrated that,” he said. “So, there are these equivalent gaps in Hong Kong law where we can already legislate now in parallel with the guidelines.”
A Security Bureau spokesman said it would closely monitor technological developments and periodically review the applicability and effectiveness of the laws to ensure they remained relevant.
Risks beyond a single response
Unlike generative artificial intelligence models that produce responses to human prompts, AI agents can independently plan, make decisions and take action over multiple stages to achieve a goal set by a user.
Singapore’s AI governance framework warns that malfunctioning agents can cause significant real-world harm. Systems involving multiple agents can amplify those risks by increasing the number of interactions.
Failures can arise from poor communication or coordination, while agents pursuing different goals can come into conflict. They may also behave in ways that appear coordinated, even without explicit instructions to work together.
“Some lessons that jurisdictions can adopt include how human oversight works best when it is both structurally embedded across the organisation and practically accessible to the people closest to the work,” said a spokesman for Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), which released the framework in January.
The spokesman said the framework addressed accountability but did not define or assign legal liability.
Many AI-related risks were already covered by Singapore’s existing legislation, he said. The guidelines provided technology-specific guidance while allowing flexibility to respond to rapid developments.

He added that the framework aimed to ensure organisations understood the risks and took appropriate action, including maintaining meaningful human control and oversight.
“Singapore’s approach has been to design frameworks that are relevant and practical for enterprises while remaining interoperable with emerging global standards,” he said.
He added that a key consideration was making the guidance applicable to businesses across all sectors while providing enough detail for them to implement it.
Mainland China’s existing AI Safety Governance Framework was updated in September by the National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity to include a chapter on agentic AI risk management.
Tailoring safeguards to Hong Kong
Mak said Hong Kong could draw several basic principles from the Singapore and mainland guidelines. These included defining agents’ authority and permissions, tracking them throughout their life cycles, logging their decisions and maintaining audit trails, particularly for multi-agent systems.
He added that the guidelines should also establish requirements for human oversight and accountability.
“So even if you have agents making decisions where they are irreversible or with very serious consequences, the human should have those decisions escalated [to them],” he said.
While the mainland framework identified categories of risk and technical countermeasures, Mak said Hong Kong’s guidelines should also address hazards specific to the city.
These included risks arising in financial regulatory sandboxes – controlled environments in which new technology or services can be tested – and from AI-equipped driverless buses due to connect the airport’s new Terminal 2 with the city’s border checkpoint of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge.
He said the city should also develop practical, open-source toolkit that businesses could download and apply to their AI systems.
He added that mainland AI apps were subject to mandatory filing with authorities and quarterly reviews, with non-compliant apps removed.
Mak described this as a model centred on pre-launch filing obligations, rather than the after-the-fact enforcement seen in some Western jurisdictions, although its market impact remained to be seen.
“So for Hong Kong, that also requires some studying for the local circumstances. But that is an approach that the Hong Kong government may want to look into as well,” he said.
Neil Tan, founder and chairman of the Artificial Intelligence Association of Hong Kong (AIHK), said, however, that the mainland’s pre-registration mechanism applied to AI models, which were released relatively infrequently, rather than agents.
He said extending mandatory filing to agents would be costly and time-consuming because there were hundreds of them.

Tan added that the association planned to release guidelines this week after almost a year of work, including a dedicated section on AI agents.
The guidelines would set out best practices for managing AI and agents across sectors including retail, logistics, transport and healthcare, he said.
Tan also expected the government’s framework to clarify the legal liability of companies using AI agents and include more case studies relevant to the public.
For example, he said, people would expect clear consumer protections if an agent mishandled an automated investment and caused substantial financial losses. If an agent mismanaged a medical appointment system, delaying critical care and resulting in a patient’s death, legal liability would also need to be addressed.
Tan, who is also the founder and managing director of AI and technology consultancy Tsunami Advisors, said the industry already had strong self-governance and self-regulation.
“For our folks, I would be very surprised if those guidelines were even stricter than they already do to themselves,” he said.
But Tan said small and medium-sized enterprises, which he described as making up more than 90 per cent of Hong Kong’s economy, were concerned about compliance costs.
He added that accommodating businesses of different sizes would be difficult for the government.
Tan said the city would also need to strike a balance between guidelines that were too restrictive and those that were too permissive to avoid undermining its appeal to international investors.


Mak said the mainland’s vibrant AI industry, despite its extensive rules and regulations, challenged the common Western argument that regulation deterred investment.
“One suggestion is that the rules are very clear as to where the red lines are, what you can and cannot do. That also encourages the industry,” he said.
An Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau spokesman said the government would draw on guidelines from other jurisdictions and consult a broad range of stakeholders to ensure its framework suited Hong Kong.
The guidelines would provide practical guidance across sectors, helping organisations identify, prevent and manage risks from AI agents. They would also help organisations establish safeguards proportionate to the nature and potential impact of their applications.
Gaps in legal liability
Mak said liability in Hong Kong would normally depend on factors such as who had a contract with the victim, whether anyone had been negligent and whether there had been criminal intent. But AI could expose gaps in that framework.
“AI isn’t a legal person, so AI itself can never be liable,” he said. “In some cases, there’s a gap where no human is also liable. Everyone has reasonable care in the chain. There’s no criminal intent. But still, the AI agent is able to cause harm.”
Mak said he expected the Department of Justice’s working group to identify such gaps. But he said the city also needed to address cross-border disputes involving overseas AI models, where compelling witnesses to appear in Hong Kong, obtaining evidence and proving causation could be difficult.
He said Hong Kong should explore insurance arrangements, potentially including mandatory cover, that would allow victims to receive compensation before liability was resolved.
But he cautioned that mandatory insurance could deter investment and that it remained unclear how such a system would work.
A Department of Justice spokesman said a cross-departmental working group had been established to examine legal liability for accidents caused by AI products. Bureaus and departments had largely completed a preliminary review of more than 600 ordinances within their policy areas.
He said the working group would shortly begin examining whether existing laws adequately addressed liability for accidents or damage caused by AI products. It would also consider legislative and regulatory responses, including guidelines.
Asked about mandatory third-party liability insurance for the use of AI products, the bureau spokesman said it would consider policy measures in light of the department’s review and developments in AI technology and its applications.

data.title: Hong Kong set for more diverse IPO pipeline in 2027, Citigroup says
data.description:
The Hong Kong stock market’s initial public offering (IPO) pipeline is set to become more diverse in 2027 as global investors will show a greater appetite for solid Chinese companies in fields including biotechnology, advanced manufacturing and renewable energy, according to Citigroup.
As demand for artificial intelligence-related equities waned, international institutions would remain keen to allocate a large portion of their assets to China’s world-beaters when they listed in Hong Kong, said Simon Yuan, Citigroup’s head of China investment banking.
“We have observed that the biotech and biomedical sectors have been relatively quiet this year, a contrast to the high level of funding activities seen last year,” he said in a media briefing on Wednesday.
“However, this momentum could return. Should China’s overall macroeconomic situation improve, we may see a resurgence in areas like advanced manufacturing and consumer businesses.”
He added that leading players in China’s renewable energy industry were also investment darlings for international asset managers.
Hong Kong’s IPO market has been bolstered this year by investors flocking to AI firms from mainland China amid belief in their technological strength and profit potential.
By the end of September, 118 companies had completed listings on the Hong Kong exchange, raising a combined HK$388 billion (US$49.5 billion) to mark a record nine-month fundraising period.
Bubble worries and expectations for tightened scrutiny over the AI industry could siphon off some buying interest in companies engaging with data centres and cloud computing in the near future, according to analysts.
But Yuan said Hong Kong’s IPO market outlook remained bullish next year because of mainland companies’ fundraising demand and global investors’ needs to diversify assets.
Should China’s overall macroeconomic situation improve, we may see a resurgence in areas like advanced manufacturing and consumer businesses
Simon Yuan, Citigroup
In September, Bonnie Chan Yiting, CEO of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), said at the bourse operator’s conference in Shanghai that mainland companies’ interest in listings was growing as a wave of firms looked to go global.
Those companies not only looked to obtain financing support in Hong Kong but hoped to connect with global capital, customers and business partners via Hong Kong to accelerate their expansion in overseas markets, she added.
Toh Jianxun, head of corporate banking at Citi for Japan, Asia North and Australia, said in the briefing that mainland firms’ go-global efforts had been the key growth driver for the company’s China business.
Citi’s “China Desk” division planned to increase staffing by 20 per cent to serve Chinese clients looking to invest in markets across the world, including those in Latin America, the Middle East and Europe.
Last month, Citi became the seventh foreign player to obtain a licence from the Chinese securities regulator to establish a fully foreign-owned brokerage in the mainland market, allowing it to offer investment banking, equities brokering, securities research and investment advisory services.
On Tuesday, global CEO Jane Fraser said at the Citi China Conference in Shanghai that the US financial services giant would become a leading investment bank in mainland China, bolstered by Beijing’s supportive stance as well as the country’s strength in manufacturing and AI.

data.title: How deep are Nvidia-linked executive Alice Huang’s Hong Kong business ties?
data.description:
Alice Huang, the Chinese tech executive accused of having an affair with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang while allegedly spying for Beijing, has ties to Hong Kong dating back about two decades – and a web of business links in the city, the South China Morning Post has found.
Huang, also known as Huang Le, first set foot in the city 20 years ago to study. Two decades on, company records show she continues to have links to the city, including as a director of a firm that shares an address with a Russian-linked robotics company sanctioned by the United States.
Described by a former classmate as “pure” and “kittenish” during her time as a student, Huang studied in Hong Kong for a master’s degree before rising to become an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International in 2023 – a company that has since faced US scrutiny over suspected attempts to circumvent export controls on advanced semiconductors.

According to sources, Huang was among the first batch of graduates from Baptist University’s master of social sciences in media management programme in 2007.
“Back then, she could speak simple English. It wasn’t very fluent but good enough for basic conversation,” a classmate from her master’s course told the SCMP. “She was also very gentle and kittenish. Her Mandarin was pleasing to listen to.”
According to the classmate, Huang was a good student who was “pure” and “cute”.
They were taught by the late Clarence Chang Ching-po, a veteran media professional and the husband of local actress Siao Fong-fong.
Following graduation, Huang worked for Hunan Satellite TV, the classmate said.
After a short career in the media industry, Huang reportedly moved into finance, working for HSBC’s private bank in Hong Kong and Citic Securities.


Her role as the managing director of Megaspeed International and her alleged romantic relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang drew global attention last month after The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by China to gather information about the chip giant and its co-founder.
Video clips showing Jensen Huang and Alice Huang together at a dinner in Taipei in May 2025 subsequently went viral, capturing the CEO with his arm around her as she kissed him on the cheek.
Beijing dismissed the allegations on Monday. “The ‘Chinese spy’ allegation was purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular press briefing.

As of Wednesday, Huang Le was registered as the director of three companies using her Hong Kong ID – Nanjing Lingxing Technology, Stag Bay Technology and Aspen Creek – according to the Hong Kong Companies Registry. The latter two were incorporated in Hong Kong in July and August this year, respectively.
Stag Bay Technology was incorporated on July 6. The company’s registered office address matches Huang’s registered address: Room 401, 4/F, Wan Chai Central Building, 89 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai.
This same address appears on a sanctions list maintained by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control targeting entities accused of conducting “harmful foreign activities” on behalf of the Russian government. The sanctioned entity sharing the address is Robotronix Semiconductors.
The address is occupied by Centrium Bright Corporate Services, a secretarial company registered as a trust or company service provider licensee in Hong Kong.
Separately, Huang registered a different address, a residential building in Sheung Wan, for Aspen Creek. The specific business activities of both Stag Bay and Aspen Creek are unknown.
Nanjing Lingxing Technology was incorporated in mainland China and established a business presence in Hong Kong in April this year. Huang Le is one of its directors in the city.
She was reportedly an investor in Nanjing Lingxing with her husband, Kang Wei. The two were seen visiting China Automotive Innovation Corporation in 2023, with other senior executives of the company.
Nanjing Lingxing operates a ride-hailing service known as T3GO on the mainland. According to its website, the company was established jointly by China FAW Group, Dongfeng Motor Corporation and Chongqing Changan Automobile, in partnership with enterprises including Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings.
Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
A company formerly controlled by Huang, 7Road International, reportedly invested more than 100 million yuan (US$15 million) to acquire a minority stake in Nanjing Lingxing in December 2024.
In April 2026, Nanjing Lingxing filed for an initial public offering on the Hong Kong stock exchange with a valuation of 24.2 billion yuan. But in September, the China Securities Regulatory Commission halted the listing, requesting further explanations on matters including historical capital increases, equity transfer pricing and pricing rationales.
Information from Singapore’s Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority showed that Megaspeed was formerly known as 7Road International.
Huang Le, who registered the company using her Hong Kong passport, was appointed director and managing director on March 6, 2023, but ceased to hold both positions on November 10 that year.
On the same day, a British Virgin Islands entity named Huang Le Limited transferred shares in Megaspeed to SwiftData, a Singapore company.
SwiftData’s sole shareholder and director, Tan Yong Pong, also known as Chen Yongpeng, was appointed a director of Megaspeed that day.
In a separate deal in 2019, the Hong Kong-listed 7Road Holdings agreed to pay 1 billion yuan to acquire a game company, Osmanthus Vale, from Malus Vale Holdings, a company wholly owned by Huang Le, according to filings with the stock exchange.
Osmanthus Vale also owned a Hong Kong company, Hawthorn Vale Holdings (Hong Kong), and its mainland subsidiaries through another entity, Malus Vale Holdings. Kang Wei, who was reportedly Huang Le’s husband, was the director of Hawthorn Vale until he resigned on May 3, 2021, according to the Hong Kong Companies Registry.
Osmanthus Vale also held a 51 per cent stake in Poplar Vale Holdings, a British Virgin Islands company, the document showed.
Alice Huang’s whereabouts are currently unknown, and she has not made any public statement about the scandal, while the Nvidia boss has promised to cooperate with a Congressional investigation in the US.

data.title: A Chinese Maserati? Huawei-backed EV firm nears pact, sources say
data.description:
Chinese luxury electric vehicle (EV) brand Maextro is moving closer to a tie-up with Italian marque Maserati, which would result in co-developed models intended to challenge the likes of BMW and Mercedes-Benz globally, according to industry sources.
Maextro, backed by technology giant Huawei Technologies, aimed to enlist Maserati’s design capabilities, styling and brand awareness to develop electric cars that could woo wealthy consumers, said two sources with knowledge of the matter.
The partners expected to mass-produce a new model by late 2027, which would be sold both in mainland China and abroad, with deliveries outside the mainland carrying Maserati badges, they added. Netherlands-based car giant Stellantis owns Maserati.
The expected deal added to evidence that international carmakers were keen on leveraging China’s EV technology, analysts said.
Maextro’s current cars – some of the most expensive on the market in China – are jointly developed by Huawei and state-owned carmaker JAC Group, which assembles the vehicles. Huawei, through its Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, supplies technology for smart driving and digital cockpits.
“Carmakers and supply-chain vendors worldwide are still looking to marry international brands with Chinese production to make and sell more electric cars,” said Phate Zhang, founder of Shanghai-based industry data ­provider CnEVPost. “Petrol cars will see a further loss of market share in both China and abroad.”
With Chinese assemblers and supply-chain vendors at the vanguard of EV technology and production, international names such as Volkswagen and Hyundai have already heavily invested in mainland-based research and development facilities to vie for bigger market share.
Leading Chinese EV makers including BYD, Geely, Leapmotor and Nio have been striving to move up the value chain through the rapid adoption of technological advances, even as they contend with suppressed consumer demand in the world’s largest automotive market.


In October, a total of 1.64 million petrol and electric cars were handed over to customers on the mainland, down 27.1 per cent year on year, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association.
For the first 10 months of this year, domestic car deliveries fell 22.3 per cent from a year earlier to just under 16 million units.
Maextro faced a safety incident last month after ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi released a video showing that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 multipurpose vehicles used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h.
Three state authorities including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) set up a joint investigation team in mid-October to verify facts regarding the incident.

data.title: China’s Huawei to roll out new phone brand Osta, 6 years after giving up Honor
data.description:
Huawei Technologies is preparing to launch a new smartphone brand, doubling down on its hard-won domestic comeback six years after spinning off budget marque Honor under the weight of US sanctions.
Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s Consumer Business Group, confirmed in a social media post on Wednesday that the company would officially debut Osta, known as “Xingmang” in Chinese, on November 20.
The unveiling will coincide with Huawei’s latest electric vehicle launches, according to Yu’s post on Weibo. Notably, the post carried a device tag showing it was sent from an “Osta O1 Pro”, a model previously identified by tech bloggers as the sub-brand’s first bar-style handset.
Online leaks suggested the device would feature a widescreen design with a display resembling that of Huawei’s flagship Pura X View.
Huawei did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
The arrival of Osta marks Huawei’s first major sub-brand venture since late 2020, when the Shenzhen-based company sold Honor to a consortium of more than 30 agents and dealers to insulate the unit from crippling US trade sanctions that blocked access to advanced chips.
After seeing its smartphone business brought close to a standstill by Washington’s restrictions, Huawei has accelerated its recovery since the late-2023 roll-out of the Mate 60 Pro, powered by an in-house Kirin processor.
The company had since regained the top spot in China’s smartphone market, capturing a 21.3 per cent share in the third quarter of 2026, ahead of Apple, with 19.5 per cent, and local rivals Vivo, Oppo, Xiaomi and former unit Honor, according to Counterpoint Research.
The expansion comes as smartphone makers contend with rising component costs and intensifying competition in the domestic market.
Alongside its push in mobile devices, Huawei is also stepping up its artificial intelligence infrastructure ambitions.
The company was preparing the commercial launch of a magneto-electric storage (MES) system designed for warm and cold data – referring to occasionally accessed and archival files, respectively – Chinese financial media outlet Yicai reported on Tuesday.
The MES architecture is positioned as a more cost-efficient and high-performance alternative to traditional hard disk drives for enterprise workloads.
Huawei was scheduled to unveil the system to commercial trial clients during a closed-door briefing on Thursday, according to a person familiar with the matter.

data.title: 30 Japanese porn stars denied entry into Hong Kong, forcing expo’s cancellation
data.description:
A large-scale adult entertainment expo billed as Hong Kong’s first has abruptly been cancelled after nearly 30 Japanese adult-video (AV) performers were refused entry upon arrival at Hong Kong International Airport.
Organisers of the “Mega Fans Expo 2026” (MFE) released a statement on Wednesday announcing with regret the immediate cancellation of the three-day show, scheduled for Friday to Sunday at the Regal Airport Hotel, as well as a preview event on Thursday.
The statement did not give a reason for the abrupt cancellation, saying only that refund arrangements would be disclosed later through official channels.
The disruption came less than 48 hours before the expo was due to open, after high-profile AV performers scheduled to appear revealed they had been denied clearance at border control and were allegedly being deported back to Japan.
Among nearly 30 guest performers – including Hibiki Otsuki, Rena Miyashita and Hikari Aozora – several took to social media to voice their shock.
Otsuki said that despite obtaining the relevant visas in advance, immigration officers turned away her manager, crew and accompanying performers upon arrival.
“This is the first time something like this has happened; I was shocked,” she wrote, describing the situation as a deepening mystery with no clear reason provided.
Miyashita also told followers online that the entire contingent appeared to face compulsory repatriation.

Industry legend Yui Hatano, who was scheduled to serve as master of ceremonies, confirmed her sudden return on social media, expressing deep regret to fans waiting at the airport and across Hong Kong.
“To everyone who was looking forward to this, I am truly sorry that things ended up turning out this way,” she said.
Legendary Japanese adult film actor Taka Kato was also scheduled to co-host the event as a special guest alongside Hatano.
The abrupt mass turnaround has left thousands of MFE ticket holders in limbo, particularly those who had paid for premium add-on experiences, including official handprint sessions priced at HK$2,380 (US$300) or HK$2,580 and meet-and-greet sessions priced at HK$1,280 or HK$1,580.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the Immigration Department for comment.
Under Hong Kong immigration rules, overseas visitors cannot ordinarily take up employment – paid or unpaid – while admitted as visitors.
A commercial performance, paid appearance or paid fan meeting may therefore require the performer to hold an appropriate employment visa or entry permit before travelling to Hong Kong, unless the activity falls within an applicable immigration facilitation arrangement.
Holding a visa or enjoying visa-free access does not guarantee entry. Immigration officers assess each arrival independently and may refuse permission to land if the person’s stated purpose, supporting documents or actual intentions do not match the conditions of their entry.

data.title: Garage owner, 72, dies after car falls on him in Hong Kong
data.description:
A 72-year-old garage owner has died after a car he was repairing fell on him in Hong Kong.
Police received a report from a passer-by at 2.50pm on Wednesday that a man had become trapped beneath a private car off Wing Lai Road in Tseung Kwan O Upper Village.
Emergency personnel arrived to find the man unconscious, with his upper body trapped under the vehicle and only part of his legs visible.
He was rescued and taken to Tseung Kwan O Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 5.03pm.
The man had reportedly raised the car with a jack and was working near its rear when it malfunctioned, causing the vehicle to fall and crush him.
Police officers were seen investigating the scene.
